newsitem.title: CANADA: Japan reform short-run minus for yen -- ex-BOJ exec.
newsitem.headline: Japan reform short-run minus for yen -- ex-BOJ exec.

text.p: The financial reform program proposed by Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto in November 1996 could prompt a short-term outflow of funds that could exert downward pressure on the yen, said Mikio Wakatsuki, former executive director at the Bank of Japan.

"In the short run, outflow may become larger, especially as the reform will take a longer time to be completed," said Wakatsuki, currently chairman of the Board of Counselors, Japan Research Institute Ltd.

"As a result, downward pressure on the exchange rate of the yen may be greater," he told an audience of foreign exchange dealers at the 39th annual congress of the Association Cambiste Internationale.
Over the medium- to long-term, Wakatsuki said that the impact of reforms on the exchange rate would become largely neutral.
"There will be a healthy two-way flow of capital once the Tokyo market becomes fully internationalized and offers more attractive investment instruments and opportunities to non- residents."
In response to questions about Japan's ailing financial sector, Wakatsuki said that bad loans among Japanese institutions had complicated the reform process.
"Those (institutions) delaying writing off bad loans will be in a very difficult situation," he added.
Japan's reform program, known as the "Big Bang," is designed to overhaul the financial system in accordance with the changing needs of international and domestic customers, Wakatsuki said.
"It is increasingly recognized by people that the Japanese economy needs to be fundamentally overhauled and reformed in order to be reinvigorated," he concluded.
